plates.caption: of what a weather radar saw above it that week: it starts in the air the radar sampled, within 50 km of it, and runs on at the heading and ground speed the radar measured, carried for 8 hours — an assumption, so a stroke reads as a flight. More strokes, more of it. Not one night and not one kind of animal: the radar cannot tell birds from bats from insects.
plates.credit: Map: Natural Earth — 1:10m land, coastline and rivers (Public domain).
plates.lead: Each stroke is one night's flight

plates.caption: by 170 foxes, drawn a day at a time from its daily median position, the red nib where it has got to in its own journey. All of them start together on day one: the published tracks carry no dates, so this is no one season. A few journeys run off the plate.
plates.credit: Map: Natural Earth — 1:10m land, coastline and rivers (Public domain).
plates.lead: Each line is one of 217 journeys

plates.caption: were recorded that week, the dashed ones the weeks before. Each stroke joins a place reached this week to the nearest place held the week before: the shift between two weekly maps, not an animal's path. One 0.01° cell is the unit, so an animal crossing three cells is in all three.

stills.caption: The more of them, the larger the dot, over the whole period at once and on a logarithmic scale, so a cell with a thousand is not drawn a thousand times the size of one. It shows where animals were tagged and followed, which is where researchers worked, as much as where animals go.
stills.credit: Data: MegaMove — global space use of marine megafauna (CC0 1.0). Published at source resolution.
stills.lead: Each dot is a one-degree cell where tracked animals were.
stills.name: marine-space-use
stills.title: Where tracked sea animals went

stills.caption: It counts what people have seen and reported, so the busiest cells are the best surveyed, and a blank cell is one with no record of these animals, not one with nothing in it.
stills.credit: Data: OBIS speciesgrids — gridded marine species distributions (H3 level 7) (CC BY 4.0). Published at source resolution.
stills.lead: Each dot is a one-degree cell, larger where more kinds of moving sea animal have at least one record.
stills.name: marine-taxa-recorded
stills.title: How many kinds of sea animal have been recorded

stills.caption: The larger the mark, the larger the change. A before and an after, not a trend, and a hole is a place nobody atlassed twice.
stills.credit: Data: Southern African Bird Atlas Project (SABAP1) — atlas cards, 1987–1991 (CC BY 4.0). Published at source resolution.
stills.lead: A solid dot is a quarter-degree cell where the second atlas recorded more kinds than the first, a ring one where it recorded fewer.
stills.name: atlas-taxa-change
